transcript.question: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from start to finish?
transcript.answer: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. Throughout the day, I add new drones to the fleet, retire old ones, and set up charging pads at our sites. I also take drones out of service for repairs, put them back when they are fixed, and send drones to charge.

What differences are there among the drones or charging pads you work with?
transcript.answer: We run several hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers. They differ in their carrying capacity, flight range on a full battery, carried sensors like cameras, thermal cameras, and laser scanners, and the charging connector types they use, which are not interchangeable. Each of our sites has its own charging pads, a few dozen in total.

transcript.question: How do the charging pads differ from one another, or across your sites?
transcript.answer: Our drones use several charging connector types that are not interchangeable. We have a few dozen charging pads at our own sites. Pads are never lent to another company.

transcript.question: Can a charging pad break or go offline, and how do you handle it when that happens?
How does your work connect with the dispatchers or the airspace desk at your company?

transcript.answer: Each drone has a home site, and we run a few dozen charging pads at our sites. We keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and repairs and servicing are carried out by us. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.

transcript.question: What exactly do regulators ask to see about how your drones have been looked after?
Can a drone charge at any of your sites, or only at its home site?
What kind of servicing or scheduled maintenance do your drones or charging pads require?
Which kind of drone operating company do you work for, and what kind of sites do you operate?
transcript.answer: I don't know which kind of drone operating company I work for among our customers, which include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. We do set up charging pads at our company's sites.

transcript.question: Is there anything else about your fleet, batteries, or sites that is important in your work?
transcript.answer: We run a few hundred drones of several models from different manufacturers that differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. Each drone has a home site, and we run a few dozen charging pads at our sites.

transcript.question: How do you manage batteries, charging progress, or taking a charging pad out of service?
transcript.answer: I send drones to charge and keep our charging equipment in working order. I don't know how to manage batteries, charging progress, or taking a charging pad out of service.

transcript.question: Is there anything else you do or deal with in your role that we have not talked about yet?
transcript.answer: I carry out repairs and servicing for our drones.

transcript.answer: My notes do not describe a worst day or how bad it was, but I do worry about the server crashing while drones are flying, especially since the platform company updates and restarts it during working hours and it occasionally crashes. I also worry about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and about closures being amended during the day.

transcript.question: Right after the server comes back up from a crash or a closure comes into force mid-flight, what do you need to find out first?
Thinking about airspace closures being amended during the day, could you give me a concrete example of how a closure changes and how that affects your flights?
transcript.answer: A closure can change when an area is widened or an end time moves, and this can happen while drones of several companies are already in the air.

transcript.question: Is there anything in your work today that you check by hand because you do not trust the system or the information you get?
Thinking about a new service being built for your work, what are you most afraid it would get wrong?
transcript.answer: I am most afraid that software might choose a drone or a way for us, because our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. Choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher.

transcript.question: Could you walk me through how you choose a drone and the way it flies for a job today?
transcript.answer: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Then I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves.

transcript.question: What determines whether one of your drones could get to where a job starts?
transcript.answer: A drone's model determines how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses. Batteries also drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

transcript.question: Besides the drone's model and the weather, what else do you check about a specific drone or its location before signing off a flight?
Could you tell me more about the jobs themselves—what information comes with a job when you start planning it?
transcript.answer: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

transcript.question: How do those limits on take-off and landing places—and charging connectors—affect how you plan a flight?
transcript.answer: Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time, and several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. Batteries and charging connectors also matter, since several connector types are in use and they are not interchangeable, and each company has its own charging pads at its own sites which are never lent to another company.

transcript.question: What happens when two dispatchers try to plan for the same popular drone or the same busy site at the same time?
What happens when a flight is in the air and something goes wrong—like a battery draining faster than planned or an airspace closure changing?
transcript.answer: I can call off a flight, since I am the licensed person responsible for each flight and a dispatcher can call off a flight. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and people and devices outside the company report whether the load is ready, whether the drone reaches the points of its job, and whether the drone arrives.

transcript.question: How do you interact with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk in your work?
Could you tell me more about those reports from people and devices outside the company—how do they reach you, and what do you do with them?
transcript.answer: Reports from drones come through relay stations, but radio coverage is patchy, so reports can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. People and devices outside the company report whether the load is ready, whether the drone reaches the points of its job, and whether the drone arrives.

transcript.question: When something goes wrong on a flight—or when reports arrive late, out of order, or not at all—what information do you or others look at afterwards?
How do airspace rules or corridors affect the way you choose for a drone to fly?
transcript.answer: The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

transcript.question: Are there any rules about who can see your company's flights, sites, or jobs, or what you can see of other companies?
transcript.answer: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

transcript.question: How do you know which drones in your fleet are fit to fly or currently available when you are planning?
What happens to a drone or a job after a flight arrives at its destination or gets called off?
Are there any legal, audit, or safety records that have to be kept about your sign-offs, flights, or decisions?
How do timing, schedules, or deadlines factor into the deliveries and inspections you dispatch?
Can a drone stop along its way at an intermediate site to charge, or how does getting to where a job starts work when a drone is somewhere else?
Is there anything else about your work as a dispatcher, your sites, your drones, or the problems you deal with that we haven't touched on yet?
transcript.answer: I worry about batteries draining faster in cold and wind than planned, and about instructions sent to drones and charging equipment not arriving or arriving twice when the sender cannot tell if the first attempt got through. I also worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, which causes reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

transcript.question: What kinds of instructions are sent to drones and charging equipment, and what happens if an instruction arrives twice or not at all?
